The over-reliance on generic tropes, however, becomes tiring. Intertextual references abound – think Tarantino, TV advertising, Bad Boys (1995), Source Code (2011), Get Out (2017), music videos – and there are contrived philosophical discussions about the original 1940s Thomas the Tank Engine book. But Bullet Train has nothing new to say about the things it’s referencing, and so the result is surface-level pastiche repackaged with a hyper-pop soundtrack. That it’s targeting online audiences is clear: with an eye on its own virality, it switches between whiplash edits and slow motion in scenes that can be pasted directly to social media. Bullet Train is like macaroni salad. When taken separately, the two items are not out of the ordinary. They are well-known and heavily relied upon by the general public. When they are combined, it congeals into a revolting substance where only those with strong convictions may partake. I believe the same is true with Bullet Train , which, taken at face value, sounds like a fun movie. Somehow, though, David Leitch's best efforts end up overcooked, underwritten, and wholly unsatisfying. For some unexplainable reason, Leitch and screenwriter Zak Olkewicz have decided, after little-to-no consideration, that the audience is not to be trusted—that is, every fifteen minutes or so we must cut back to an event that occurred anywhere from just half an hour to twenty-six years ago. Whether the viewer needed to see this abrupt change in setting is of course, up to Leitch, who also believed a quick injection of Quentin Tarantino's quippy dialogue was suitable for this film. It turned out to be one of the main detractors, constantly bookending the more fun action scenes with truly unnecessary flair. I respect Leitch's attempt, but the entire effort falls flat as Brad Pitt struggles to keep a sinking ship afloat.

Oftentimes I make this distinction in reviewing media that it’s either good (aka serious and complicated) or fun (aka easy on the brain and quickly dopamine-inducing). Most action movies I lump in the second box, and I don’t often complain about them not being good enough, because I get the purpose they serve for audiences. I also understand for a movie around 2 hours to land effectively, making it very entertaining is a sort of shortcut to sell people on it when the narrative isn’t up to par. It would be pretentious and wrong of me to claim being above dumb fun movies when my watched catalogue overwhelmingly consists of them, but the downside of these is that I leave the movie theater with not much of anything to say beyond “it was fun”. Therefore, it’s interesting to me when I have so much praise for an action movie that I can express in a meaningful way. Bullet Train is probably among the few movies in this genre that you will see on this list, and it’s through impressively clever and efficient writing that it squeezes so many things to love in such a short time. The movie from start to finish almost bombards you with plot elements, moving parts to the story ranging from throwaway dialogue lines to big actions like character deaths that have rippling effects on the rest of the story. Much like its location, it doesn’t slow down for a single second, making for an absolutely thrilling watching experience that fits in a staggering number of “OH SHIT I REMEMBER THAT FROM EARLIER IN THE MOVIE”. With no exaggeration EVERYTHING in this movie has a logical cause and effect and because it manages to stick the landing beautifully while tying all its loose ends together, it never feels overwhelming, even on first watch. It’s chock-full of small details that enrich every subsequent rewatch, and in this way it cements itself in the space of streaming services by making the re-experiencing of the story so close to the cinema viewing experience. At the same time, the movie is a beautiful example of avoiding tonal disonnance, a problem I have frequently with comedy action stories. Bullet train is a comedy first, drama second, but the serious moments work really well because of the character work around them. I have to point out how impressive it is to introduce so many characters in the span of a 2 hour movie, some of whom die in less than 15 minutes, that all evoke the sense they have more to their story than what’s presented. In the Wolf’s and Hornet’s first appearances, the movie disguises effective, concise exposition under the comedy of a rapid-fire flashback introduction that you would see in a much worse movie. This ability to work both fronts at the same time in comedy and storytelling with every character interaction is what allows them the freedom of multitudes, where tragic moments like Lemon’s death are given the necessary space to not feel jarring against the other light-hearted parts. The characters are, obviously, ridiculous to a point, exaggerated in fun ways, but not to the degree that they become one-trait caricatures (yes, including the oni-mask russian crime lord named the White Death). In the sharp contrast of these characters, where Ladybug, Prince and the Father feel like they could be from 3 different genres of movies, lie the most hillarious moments of the film that work in tandem with the foreshadowed elements to continously drive the plot forward, all the way to a bombastic ending with a villain death so amazingly anti-climactic you can’t help but want more. And yet, it’s over in the above mentioned runtime, and it’s impossible for it to overstay its welcome or ever get boring. I love Bullet Train a lot, and it’s a staple in my rotation of movies/shows I could rewatch for comfort dozens of times before I get bored. It has a very tight, well-written script that elevates it from a dumb fun action movie to a secret third thing: intelligent fun action movie. Please let this movie be one that gets milked to death with 10 more slightly worse sequels, I will be seated for all of them.

Chekhov's gun the movie. I have a weird relationship with this film. It’s one of those films I find to be very very mid, but I always remember it for some reason. And I want to like it more than I actually do. Like this film has all the stuff I like. A director and actors I like. A premise I like. A setting I like. It has bad people, doing bad things, in a bad world. Assassins, murderers, and criminals all confined in a small place, trying to get the same things. But this movie falls flat for me in a lot of areas. I find the action besides the ending to be very OK at best and bad at worst. I find the comedy only works with lemon and tangerine and no one else. The product placements are egregious. The editing does not trust the audience to remember stuff that was actually established within the dialogue. They got a Puerto Rican dude to play a Mexican to be barely in the movie. And one of my biggest complaints is Brad Pitt is absolutely dog shit in this movie. He’s unfunny. Completely unconvincing in the role. Like an asshole I read the book after watching the movie for the first time. And besides the fact, this is a sequel to another book so I had to read two books. Ladybug in the book is an unlucky fuck up, but he is competent at doing his job and not spouting unfunny therapy quotes. Aaron Taylor-Johnson is the standout of this movie if he does get to play James Bond it’s because of this film. He’s believable in the action scenes. He’s funny. And he’s just bad ass. Brian Henry as lemon is funny and steals the movie and all the scenes he is in. And finally Joey King is great as Prince in this movie. In the book the character is like a 12 year-old boy and I think the sex change honestly makes the character better. I don’t really care that the movie decided to be far more international than the very Japanese cast of the book. What it does make like the world building really unbelievable like in the book I believe that like all these seemingly pretty small scale assassins and criminals would be on this bullet train. Also, I kinda like how the book version weaves some of the characters from the first book in it. I also feel like it’s just a More self-assured story where the movie is very much trying to be more smarter than it is. I think the ending in the movie works for what it’s trying to do it’s big, It’s bombastic and it’s violent but I feel like the books is far more satisfying in a weird way. The books ending is definitely a bit underwhelming, but I think that’s a problem for all of his books because that happened in the first one as well. And also the celebrity cameos in this movie are also quite bad. I feel like giving roles to famous actors and musicians it’s fine, but why is Channing Tatum here to just make gay jokes. Why is Ryan Reynolds even get a cameo at the end? It feels like this movie had far too big of a budget and they needed to use it somehow. And honestly, yeah that is probably the problem. They made a pretty small stake story about a bunch of assassins on a train, and into a far too loud and bombastic Hollywood film. I kind of wish I would like to see a small Indy team try to do this story. For the pure fact that this movie has so many memes that still pop up every once in a while, it’s clear this movie did something right. Would I recommend it? Sure you could waste your time watching far worse movies. And I do enjoy parts of it, but I wish I enjoyed it more.

This is a fun film which suffers from biting off way more than it can chew. I did enjoy it a lot and felt some elements were really well done, while others fell very short. The best thing for me was the comedic acting. All the one liners and funny moments completely landed for me and I found myself actively laughing throughout. I thought the standout permanent was Aaron Taylor Johnson who was just absolutely hilarious. His back and forths as Tangerine with Lemon were outstanding and it really reminded me of Pulp Fiction in the best way. Brian Tyree Henry was great in his acting but the British accent was so so bad. I don’t know if it was kind of on purpose to be funnier but either way for me it was taking me out of the film and didn’t work at all. The action sequences also looked really good with some cool innovative moments where fight scenes felt punchier and more intense than usual. Brad Pitt was also great in this and played his part to perfection having enough to hold the movie together. The actual plot and the way the story all intertwines is what really lets the film down. There is just so much going on and nothing really substantial to mould it all together. There is also an issue with the serious moments where the films tone just doesn’t match. To me it should have just been a straight up action comedy and leave any of the deeper plot alone. I also found the direction a bit too slick and it made the movie come across as almost looking like an AI generated picture. The CGI and effects also didn’t look great. As an overall movie there is enough here to enjoy but I also wouldn’t go as far as to say I’m in a rush to see it again.
